- Model consistently overestimates prices in the early part of the forecast horizon, especially after sharp spikes or rebounds.
- Forecasts tend to be too optimistic in the first 5–10 days, then gradually drift downward — suggesting a lag in adjusting to true market dynamics.
- After a price spike, model forecasts often overshoot and remain elevated longer than actual prices, failing to reflect mean reversion.
- Model underestimates prices during sharp downward corrections or when true outcomes show sudden drops (e.g., 40+ → 35–36).
- Forecasts show poor sensitivity to recent low-price periods — fails to “learn” from recent dips and overweights prior high prices.
- Model exhibits persistent bias toward higher prices in the second half of the forecast, especially when true outcomes show a clear downward trend.
- Forecasts should be adjusted downward if the last 5–7 days of history show a clear downward trend or price correction.
- When true outcomes show a sharp reversal from high to low, model should reduce forecast slope and avoid over-optimism.
- Model tends to ignore short-term volatility and overweights long-term trends — should be calibrated to respond to recent price action more aggressively.
- Forecasts should be capped at recent low prices if the last 3–5 days show a clear downward correction — avoid “over-leveraging” upward bias.
